overview: The atlas uses “Arabs” for a broad Arabian area from about 200 to 100 BCE. This was no single kingdom. Ancient authors applied the name to different communities, and neither residence in Arabia nor a particular script identifies everyone as Arab. This card explores regional examples at Thaj and Mleiha, while keeping Saba, the Nabataean kingdom and later Arabian states distinct.

periods.title: Earlier trading centers
periods.summary: Thaj and Mleiha were already developing as important settlements before this atlas interval.

periods.title: The atlas century
periods.summary: The mapped century includes regional towns, caravan commerce and the Mleiha amphora inscription; the outline is not a single state border.

periods.title: Later local histories
periods.summary: Occupation continued after the map label ends; Mleiha survived into the third century CE, while Thaj followed its own trajectory.

sections.title: A region of communities and rulers

items.text: The imported outline reaches across much of Arabia, but it cannot show the boundaries of an ancient ethnic identity. “Arab” could mean different things to different writers. The towns discussed here are securely located regional examples; their artifacts do not establish that all their residents shared one language, ancestry or political allegiance.
Before this map interval, Gerrha negotiated with Antiochus III around 205 BCE. Polybius reports an interpreted letter requesting freedom, followed by gifts of silver and aromatics.

Gerrha’s merchants connected eastern Arabia with incense-producing southern regions and customers farther north. Potts discusses Strabo’s report of a forty-day journey to Hadramawt. That is weeks of transport and provisioning behind a pleasant smell. Gerrha’s exact location is debated; identifying it automatically with excavated Thaj would hide an important uncertainty.

Mleiha in today’s Sharjah participated in a southeastern Arabian kingdom named Oman. Its coins drew on Hellenistic models, and its position linked overland and maritime commerce. Excavator Bruno Overlaet describes Mleiha as a proposed capital: a substantial political center, but not proven ruler of the entire Arabian polygon.

At Thaj, a fortified town covered roughly forty hectares. Excavations exposed residential blocks and a monumental gateway flanked by towers. Repairs and additions eventually made part of the defenses nearly ten meters thick. Those dimensions belong to the town’s long history, rather than one construction campaign in 200 BCE.

Thaj depended on groundwater as well as trading routes. Masonry wells around the site reach a lasting karst aquifer, replenished by deeper water and rainfall. Drawing and maintaining water supplies was essential work for residents; the excavated wells make that need tangible, without supplying an invented ancient toilet system.

Thaj’s workshop landscape changed over time. At Tall al-Zayir, a pottery workshop operating in the fourth or third century BCE preceded an aristocratic cemetery of the first or second century CE. The same ground could move from making everyday vessels to commemorating the dead as the town changed.

A Mleiha farmhouse complex dated broadly to 200 BCE through 100 CE contained ovens and grinding stones for preparing cereals and bread. Its neighboring kitchen included steps descending to a chamber with two large ovens. Before a loaf reached the table, somebody had to grind, mix, tend the heat and clean up.

These kitchen remains are also evidence of learned skill: grinding grain and managing an oven required practice. They do not identify the teacher or establish a formal school. A stone grinder gives us a firmer glimpse of everyday work than guessing which family member had to do the washing up.

One Mleiha tomb preserves an unusually personal political record. An inscription names Amud and says his son built the monument for him; both appear as inspectors serving the king of Oman. Its damaged year probably corresponds to 222/221 or 215/214 BCE. It links kinship, commemoration and royal service shortly before the mapped century.

At Thaj, archaeologists used pottery to untangle layers of settlement. Thin Seleucid-style vessels and Greek black-glazed fragments helped date early levels to the third century BCE. Comparable fragments beneath the wall’s foundations linked a building project to that sequence. Broken dishes can act as archaeological clocks, though they rarely give an exact year.

A handle from a Mleiha tomb carries the scholarly transcription “ʾby / bn / hnʾyn”: “(Belonging to) ʾBY son of HNʾYN.” Written in South Arabian cursive zabūr, it marks ownership. The chamber dates to the middle second century BCE; the Rhodian-type jar was manufactured between 225 and 125 BCE. This is an ancient regional witness, not modern Arabic script.

The owner’s mark makes writing an ordinary possession-management tool, not only something kings displayed. Stein also identified related cursive writing on a silver plaque from Mleiha. He suggests that writing had broader practical uses there, while noting that everyday correspondence itself has not yet been recovered. The evidence does not tell us how many residents could read.

Mleiha’s burials also connect families with long-distance exchange. Excavations recovered imported wine containers among funerary offerings. These were deliberate choices about what accompanied the dead, rather than a census of ordinary meals. Goods traveling across seas could become part of a deeply local act of remembrance.

Fish bones show that inland Mleiha was supplied from the sea. Tuna relatives recur in well-sampled phases from the third century BCE onward. A much later example, building H in the second to mid-third century CE, contained processed fish with heads removed; researchers interpret the stock as probably salted and sun-dried for storage and transport.

The burned fish stock in building H was a discovery about both food and a building’s final days. The researchers distinguish heat from the house fire from cooking marks. That distinction matters: an accidental archaeological “roast” cannot be turned into a recipe. Nor does evidence for a burned building identify who caused the fire.

ending.text: There was no collective “fall of the Arabs” in 100 BCE. That is this imported record’s endpoint. Arabian settlements and communities continued through distinct local political and economic changes; the ancient label cannot be treated as one state with one conqueror.
